title: The Life of a Lighthouse Keeper
description: What daily life was like for the people who looked after lighthouses.
instructions: Read the passage about lighthouse keepers, then choose the best answer for each question.

paragraphs.text: For hundreds of years, lighthouses have warned ships about dangerous rocks and coastlines. Before modern technology, each lighthouse needed a keeper to make sure the light never went out. Keepers often lived in the lighthouse itself or in a small house next to it. Many of these buildings stood on lonely cliffs or tiny islands far from the nearest town.

A keeper's work was hard and never-ending. Every evening, the lamp had to be lit, and during the night it needed to be checked regularly. The glass lenses had to be cleaned carefully so that the light would shine as brightly as possible. In foggy weather, keepers also sounded a loud horn or rang a bell to warn sailors who could not see the light.

Life could be very lonely, especially on island lighthouses. Supplies such as food, fuel and letters arrived by boat, but storms sometimes stopped deliveries for weeks. To pass the time, keepers read books, painted, fished or kept detailed diaries about the weather. Some keepers lived with their families, and children sometimes helped with the daily jobs.

During the twentieth century, most lighthouses became automatic, and the job of keeper slowly disappeared. Today, lights are controlled by machines and checked from a distance. Some old lighthouses have been turned into museums or holiday homes. Visitors who climb their narrow stairs can still imagine the quiet, dedicated lives of the people who once kept the lights burning.

Not all keepers were men. In many countries, women also looked after lighthouses, often taking over the job when a husband or father became ill or died. Some of them became national heroes. In 1838, Grace Darling, the daughter of a keeper in the north of England, helped her father row through a terrible storm to rescue survivors of a shipwreck. Her story was told in newspapers, songs and paintings, and it showed how a keeper's work could go far beyond simply looking after a light.

Keepers also had to follow strict rules. They wrote down the weather, passing ships and any problems in an official logbook, and inspectors visited from time to time to check that everything was in order. On remote rock lighthouses, two or three keepers often worked together in shifts, so that someone was always awake. Every few weeks, a boat would bring a new keeper so that one of the others could go home for a rest. Living so close together for weeks could be difficult, and small disagreements could easily grow. Getting along with others was therefore almost as important as being good at the job.

Even in the age of satellite navigation, lighthouses have not lost their value. Many still work as a back-up in case electronic systems fail, and their lights remain a familiar sight for sailors. For people on land, they have also become symbols of safety, hope and guidance. Across the world, volunteer groups raise money to repair old towers and share their history with visitors. In this way, the memory of the keepers lives on, long after the last of them left their lights.

questions.text: What is the main idea of the passage?
